facts.claim: Snow blindness is sunburn of the eyes by ultraviolet light: red, gritty, very painful eyes that can't bear light. It shows only hours after the exposure, sometimes at night, and usually heals within a day; a few unprotected minutes on a glacier at altitude can cause it.

source.title: UIAA MedCom No 20: Eye Problems on Expeditions (2021) → 3. Snow blindness

versions.note: Like a welder's arc eye: it feels like sand in the eyes.

source.title: Medex: Travel at High Altitude (2008 edition) → The Eyes

facts.claim: Ultraviolet exposure rises by this much for every 300 m climbed.

facts.claim: Snow reflects this share of ultraviolet light.

source.title: UIAA MedCom No 20: Eye Problems on Expeditions (2021) → 3. Snow blindness

facts.claim: Goggles, or glasses with side pieces that block all ultraviolet, are worn in snow at all times, under cloud too; lost ones are improvised from card with thin slits, and porters need them as much as their clients.

source.title: UIAA MedCom No 20: Eye Problems on Expeditions (2021) → 3. Snow blindness

versions.note: A climber on Everest who wore sunglasses rather than goggles on summit day, with contact lenses left in for four days, saw blurred at 8,600 m and couldn't see to navigate on the summit; two Sherpas helped him down, and his sight stayed reduced for good.

source.title: Medex: Travel at High Altitude (2008 edition) → The Eyes

facts.claim: Small bleeds at the back of the eye (high-altitude retinopathy) are common and usually harmless, but one over the centre of vision blurs it; a climber who loses vision in either eye descends.

versions.note: Vision lost or a badly swollen optic disc: descend at least 300 m with oxygen; vision blurred, many bleeds or a mildly swollen disc: no higher. A swollen disc may be early HACE.

facts.claim: Frostbite begins as white, numb, hard skin; rewarming is very painful, and the skin turns red, itchy, blotchy and swollen; then come blisters, and at last black, dead skin that may cost fingers and toes.

facts.claim: Frostbite is superficial, with little or no tissue lost (first degree: redness and numbness; second: blisters of clear or milky fluid), or deep, with tissue lost (third: blue-grey skin; fourth: freezing to muscle or bone, colourless hard skin that rewarms without pain, then turns black and falls away over months).

source.title: Omidi et al. 2025, What Is New in Altitude- and Cold-Related Illnesses of Travel (a review of the WMS 2024 guidelines) → 1.6 Definitions and Epidemiology of Frostbite

facts.claim: Frostnip is a superficial injury without freezing that often comes before frostbite.

facts.claim: Frostbite is a risk below this air temperature, and more so below −15 °C.

source.title: Omidi et al. 2025, What Is New in Altitude- and Cold-Related Illnesses of Travel (a review of the WMS 2024 guidelines) → 1.7 Strategies for the Prevention of Frostbite

versions.note: In freezing temperatures and/or high winds.

facts.claim: Thin air as well as cold makes frostbite easier; so do tight boots or clothing, alcohol and some medicines, poor food and poor circulation, while exercise keeps the hands and feet warmer. Parts that stick out freeze first: fingers, toes, nose, ears, chin, lips.

source.title: Medex: Travel at High Altitude (2008 edition) → The Extremities

facts.claim: Frostbite is prevented rather than cured: kit that fits, hands and feet kept dry (wet gloves and socks changed at once), layers against cold and wind, warmers, and as little time exposed as possible.

source.title: Medex: Travel at High Altitude (2008 edition) → The Extremities

versions.note: Treatment rarely restores everything.

facts.claim: A frozen part is thawed only where it won't freeze again, since refreezing does more harm; until then it's padded, kept still and never rubbed, and the climber is got out of the cold.

facts.claim: A frozen part is rewarmed in water at this temperature, for about half an hour, until it's soft and red.
